new_statements.quote: Shina has been defined as a pitch accented language. [...] It means that every word in these varieties of Shina has one syllable that is accented or prominent in comparison to the rest of the syllables. [p. 102] [...] Every word in Gurezi has one and only one accented syllable, irrespective of whether the word is monosyllabic or polysyllabic. Complex words comprising a root morpheme and one or more suffixes can have the accented syllable either in its root morpheme or the affixed morpheme. Thus, similarly to other varieties of Shina, pitch accent in Gurezi is a lexical feature. [...] Like other varieties of Shina, it has been found in Gurezi that syllables having a long vowel always carry the accent, irrespective of their position in a word. [p. 103]
new_statements.citation: Ahmed, Musavir. 2016. A descriptive study of the phonology of Gurezi Shina. Acta Orientalia Academiae Scientiarum Hungaricae 69(1): 87-106.
new_statements.locator: §8 'Pitch Accent', pp. 102-103 (PDF pp. 16-17); minimal pairs and pitch traces pp. 103-105; also §5.1 p. 92 (/akáai/ 'eleven' vs /akaái/ 'fast')
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: extracted text confirms PDF p. 16 carries running head '102 MUSAVIR AHMED' and PDF p. 17 carries '.. GUREZI SHINA 103'). Section '8. Pitch Accent' begins on p. 102: 'Shina has been defined as a pitch accented language. The observation that Shina is a pitch accented language has been made with reference to Gilgiti (Bailey 1924; Radloff 1999), Kohistani (Schmidt - Kohistani 2008) and Palula (Liljegren 2008) varieties. It means that every word in these varieties of Shina has one syllable that is accented or prominent in comparison to the rest of the syllables.' On p. 103: 'Every word in Gurezi has one and only one accented syllable, irrespective of whether the word is monosyllabic or polysylla…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has a Shina record with an empty rule and no existing statements, so this is the first placement statement held by the project: the language is a pitch accent language with lexically contrastive accent position and a long-vowel-attracts-accent constraint. It describes the Gurezi variety (Indian Kashmir), not Gilgiti, but claims the same system holds across Shina varieties.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Gurezi Shina has a lexical pitch accent: exactly one accented syllable per word, realised as local high pitch (with a rising or falling contour), and its position is not predictable from the edge of the word (it may sit on the root or on a suffix). The one phonological constraint is weight-based: a long vowel always carries the accent regardless of position, and within the long vowel the accent may sit on either the first or the second mora, giving minimal pairs such as /pháal/ vs /phaál/, /wáai/ vs /waái/, /akáai/ 'eleven' vs /akaái/ 'fast'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; the work states one and only one accented syllable per word.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions; the mora-placement contrast within long vowels is the main complication. The author relies on Radloff (1999, pp. 57-63) for the Gilgiti description and says Gurezi 'behaves in the same manner as in Gilgiti, Kohistani and Palula'.
new_statements.identity_note: Ahmed 2016 describes Gurezi Shina (Gurez valley, District Bandipora, Jammu & Kashmir, India), not the Gilgit variety; the author explicitly states the accent system behaves the same as in Gilgiti, Kohistani and Palula. Radloff 1999 (not opened) and Radloff & Shakil 1998 (held by the project) describe Gilgiti Shina (Gilgit, Pakistan). The catalog record 'Shina' is variety-unspecified.

sources.quote: 'Each basic word in Gilgit Shina carries an accent on one syllable, which is marked by pitch (or tone or tune). Long vowels may carry High Falling /áa/ or Low Rising /aá/ pitch accent, short vowels may carry a High Short /á/ pitch accent. (The use of acute accent on the first or second member of the geminate vowel agrees with Buddruss, e.g., 1996.) In this pitch accent system, if there is a long vowel in the root or core part of the word, that long vowel will carry the accent.
